questions.stem: What is the original source of all new alleles in a population's gene pool?
options: Genetic drift
Selective breeding
Mutation
Natural selection
questions.explanation: Mutations are changes to the DNA sequence and are the only way a genuinely new allele arises. Selection, drift and selective breeding change how common existing alleles are, but they do not create new ones. Gene flow can bring alleles in, but they first arose by mutation elsewhere.

questions.stem: In a population of 200 flowering plants, 36 are aa, 48 are Aa and 116 are AA. What is the frequency of allele a?
questions.explanation: There are 400 alleles in 200 diploid plants. Allele a is carried twice by each aa plant and once by each Aa plant: (2 × 36) + 48 = 120, and 120/400 = 0.30. The answer 0.18 counts only the aa plants as a share of the 200 individuals, not of the alleles.

questions.stem: A storm kills most of a small island's lizard population at random, regardless of their traits. The survivors carry fewer alleles than the original population. What is this an example of?
options: Natural selection acting on storm resistance
A founder effect, a form of gene flow
Gene flow from a neighbouring island
A bottleneck effect, a form of genetic drift
questions.explanation: A sudden, random reduction in population size is a bottleneck, which changes allele frequencies by chance and usually lowers genetic diversity. Because the deaths were unrelated to the lizards' traits, it is not selection. A founder effect occurs when a small group starts a new population elsewhere, and it is also a form of drift, not gene flow.

questions.stem: A few birds blown off course start a new population on a remote island. A rare allele in the mainland population is common on the island. What best explains this?
options: Gene flow: birds keep moving the allele from the mainland to the island
Mutation: the island environment caused the allele to arise again
Selective breeding: the birds chose mates carrying the allele
The founder effect: the few founders happened to carry the allele
questions.explanation: The founders are a small, chance sample of the mainland gene pool, so an allele that is rare overall can be common among them, and so in the new population. That is the founder effect, a form of genetic drift. A remote island receives little gene flow, and environments do not cause particular mutations.

questions.stem: Why does genetic drift have a much greater effect on small populations than on large ones?
options: Small populations have higher mutation rates than large ones do
Selection pressures are always stronger in small populations
Gene flow is always faster in small populations than large ones
Chance events affect a larger share of a small gene pool
questions.explanation: Drift is change by chance in which individuals happen to reproduce. In a small population, the loss of a few individuals is a large fraction of the gene pool, so allele frequencies can shift sharply and alleles can be lost altogether. Mutation rates do not depend on population size.

questions.stem: Pollen from a large population of wattles regularly reaches a small, isolated population of the same species. What is the most likely effect on the small population?
options: Its allele frequencies stay fixed because pollen does not carry alleles
Its genetic diversity increases and it becomes more like the large one
Its genetic diversity falls because new alleles replace the old ones
It becomes a separate species because new alleles have arrived
questions.explanation: Pollen carries the male gametes, so it brings alleles into the small population; this gene flow adds diversity and reduces the differences between the populations. Continuing gene flow works against speciation, because it stops the two gene pools diverging.

questions.stem: Over many years, the frequency of an allele for dark colouring rises in a moth population after soot darkens the tree trunks. Which statement describes the process correctly?
options: Dark moths were eaten less by birds, so left more offspring
The soot caused mutations that made the moths' wings turn dark
Individual moths darkened during their lives to match the trunks
Birds carried the dark allele into the population from elsewhere
questions.explanation: Predation by birds is the selection pressure: dark moths on dark trunks are camouflaged, survive and reproduce more, and pass on the dark allele. The environment selects among existing variants; it does not cause the mutations, and individuals do not evolve during their lifetimes.

questions.stem: The Tasmanian devil population has very low genetic diversity. Why does this make the species more vulnerable?
options: Few individuals may carry alleles that help them survive a new threat
Low diversity makes the devils mutate faster than other species
Low diversity makes every devil more likely to be eaten by predators
Low diversity stops the devils reproducing sexually at all
questions.explanation: With little genetic variation, there is less chance that some individuals carry alleles that protect against a new disease or change in the environment. Devil facial tumour disease spreads between devils partly because their immune markers are so similar. Low diversity does not raise mutation rates or prevent sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: Which process increases the genetic diversity of a population?
options: Inbreeding between closely related individuals
Selective breeding for one desirable trait
Gene flow from another population of the same species
A bottleneck event that kills most of the population
questions.explanation: Gene flow brings in alleles that may be new to the population. Bottlenecks, inbreeding and selective breeding all tend to reduce diversity, by losing alleles or by making individuals more homozygous.

questions.stem: How does selective breeding change a gene pool?
options: The environment chooses which individuals survive and leave offspring
Mutations occur more often in the animals that humans want to breed
Humans choose which individuals breed, raising chosen alleles
Humans insert genes from other species into the chosen breeding animals
questions.explanation: In selective breeding people act as the selection pressure, allowing only individuals with wanted traits to reproduce. Inserting genes from another species is genetic modification, and selection by the environment is natural selection.

questions.stem: Many dog breeds have high rates of inherited disorders such as hip dysplasia. Which consequence of selective breeding best explains this?
options: Higher mutation rates caused by the breeding process
Gene flow between breeds that carries in new alleles
Reduced genetic diversity and more homozygous recessive individuals
Increased genetic diversity from mating with wild relatives
questions.explanation: Breeding from a few chosen individuals, often related ones, narrows the gene pool, so harmful recessive alleles are more often inherited from both parents and expressed. Breeds are kept separate, so gene flow is low, not high.

questions.stem: Breeders of Merino sheep in Australia have selected for finer wool over many generations. What change to the gene pool is expected?
options: Alleles linked to fine wool rise in frequency and overall diversity falls
Alleles linked to fine wool fall in frequency and overall diversity rises
New alleles for fine wool appear because breeders demand them
Allele frequencies stay the same because only the wool is changed
questions.explanation: Choosing fine-wooled rams and ewes as parents raises the frequency of the alleles that contribute to fine wool, while other alleles are lost from the flock, so diversity falls. Selection works on existing variation; demand does not create alleles.

questions.stem: A population of bacteria is treated with an antibiotic, and the next generation is mostly resistant. Which explanation is correct?
options: The antibiotic weakened over time, so all the bacteria survived
A few bacteria already carried resistance and survived to reproduce
The antibiotic caused mutations that made the bacteria resistant
The bacteria built up immunity by making antibodies against the drug
questions.explanation: Resistance alleles existed before treatment, from random mutation or from a plasmid passed between cells, even between species. The antibiotic is the selection pressure: it kills susceptible cells, and resistant survivors multiply. The drug does not cause the useful mutation, and bacteria do not make antibodies.

questions.stem: What is antigenic drift in the influenza virus?
options: The movement of virus particles between populations by air travel
Small, gradual changes to surface antigens from point mutations
A sudden, major change when two strains swap whole gene segments
Random changes in allele frequency in a small population of hosts
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift is the steady build-up of small mutations in the genes for surface proteins such as haemagglutinin and neuraminidase. A sudden swap of gene segments between strains is antigenic shift. Random change in small populations is genetic drift, a different idea with a similar name.

questions.stem: Why does the influenza vaccine need to be updated most years?
options: The virus becomes resistant to the vaccine as bacteria do to antibiotics
Antigenic drift changes the surface antigens that antibodies recognise
Antigenic shift happens every year and creates a new virus subtype
Memory cells made by the vaccine are destroyed within each year
questions.explanation: Small changes to the surface antigens accumulate each season, so memory cells and antibodies from last year's vaccine may no longer bind well. Antigenic shift is much rarer and produces a new subtype unpredictably, not every year.

questions.stem: Two different influenza A strains, one from birds and one from humans, infect the same pig cell. A new strain emerges with a mix of their gene segments. Why is this a greater threat than antigenic drift?
options: It produces a new subtype with antigens few people have immunity to
It produces a strain with point mutations that existing vaccines target
It produces a bacterium that is resistant to most common antibiotics
It produces a strain that can only infect pigs and not humans
questions.explanation: Antigenic shift reassorts whole gene segments, so the new strain can carry surface antigens that the human population has never met. With little existing immunity it can spread widely and cause a pandemic. Drift produces small changes, so some existing immunity usually remains.

questions.stem: In undisturbed sedimentary rock, which layers contain the oldest fossils?
options: The layers containing the most fossils
The lowest layers
The highest layers
The middle layers
questions.explanation: Sediments are deposited on top of older ones, so in undisturbed strata the deepest layers are the oldest. This principle of superposition is the basis of relative dating.

questions.stem: Which features make a fossil species useful as an index fossil?
options: It was widespread, abundant and short-lived in geological time
It was rare, found in one place and existed for a very long time
It shows features of two different groups of organisms
It contains enough carbon to be dated by carbon-14
questions.explanation: An index fossil marks a narrow time interval and can be found in many places, so rock layers containing it can be matched and dated relative to each other. Showing features of two groups describes a transitional fossil.

questions.stem: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird, but teeth, claws and a long bony tail like a reptile. What kind of fossil is it?
options: A vestigial fossil
A transitional fossil
An index fossil
A trace fossil
questions.explanation: A transitional fossil shows a mix of features from an ancestral group and a descendant group, supporting the idea that one evolved from the other. An index fossil is used to date rock layers, and its value lies in its narrow time range, not its features.

questions.stem: What does the principle of faunal succession state?
options: Fossil species appear in rock layers in a consistent order
Every rock layer contains the same species of fossil organisms
All fossils of animals are older than all fossils of plants
Fossils in higher layers are always older than those in lower layers
questions.explanation: Faunal (fossil) succession is the observation that fossil groups follow one another in the same order wherever rocks of that age are found, so layers in different places can be correlated. Older fossils lie lower, not higher, in undisturbed strata.

questions.stem: How does absolute dating of a fossil differ from relative dating?
options: It gives an age in years, using the depth of the fossil below ground
It gives only an order of age, using the species found nearby
It gives an age in years, using the decay of radioactive isotopes
It gives only an order of age, using the position of the rock layers
questions.explanation: Absolute (radiometric) dating measures the proportions of a radioactive isotope and its decay product to calculate an age in years. Relative dating only places fossils in order, older or younger, using superposition and index fossils. Depth alone cannot give an age in years.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. A bone contains 25% of the carbon-14 it had when the animal died. About how old is the bone?
options: 17 190 years
1433 years
11 460 years
5730 years
questions.explanation: After one half-life 50% remains, and after two half-lives 25% remains, so the bone is 2 × 5730 = 11 460 years old. The answer 17 190 is three half-lives, which would leave 12.5%.

questions.stem: Why is potassium–argon dating, rather than carbon-14 dating, used for a fossil about three million years old?
options: Potassium–argon dating measures carbon in the fossil itself
Carbon-14 decays too slowly to measure such a young fossil
Almost no carbon-14 would remain after so many half-lives
Carbon-14 is found only in plant fossils, not animal fossils
questions.explanation: With a half-life of 5730 years, carbon-14 falls below measurable levels after roughly 50 000 years. Potassium-40 has a half-life of over a billion years, so it suits much older samples; it is used to date volcanic layers above and below the fossil, not the fossil itself.

questions.stem: What is required for two populations to be considered separate species?
options: They look different from each other in at least one trait
They eat different foods in the same environment
They can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
They live in different places and have never met
questions.explanation: Under the biological species concept, populations are separate species when they are reproductively isolated and cannot produce fertile offspring together. Populations can look different or live apart and still be one species if they could interbreed successfully.

questions.stem: The Galapagos finches are an example of allopatric speciation. What was the key first step?
options: Finches changed their beaks during life to eat new foods
Populations were separated on different islands by ocean
Populations on the same island chose mates by flowering time
One finch was born with a mutation that made it a new species
questions.explanation: In allopatric speciation a geographical barrier, here the sea between islands, stops gene flow. Each isolated population then meets different selection pressures, such as different seeds, and diverges until reproductive isolation develops. Speciation takes many generations; one mutant does not form a species.

questions.stem: Two species of Howea palm on Lord Howe Island arose from one ancestor without a geographical barrier. What type of speciation is this?
options: Selective breeding
Sympatric speciation
Allopatric speciation
Antigenic shift
questions.explanation: Sympatric speciation happens within the same area, with no physical barrier separating the populations. On Lord Howe Island, palms on different soil types came to flower at different times, which isolated them reproductively. Allopatric speciation needs a geographical barrier.

questions.stem: On Lord Howe Island, Howea palms growing on different soils came to flower at different times. Why did this lead to speciation?
options: The soils caused mutations that made the palms unable to reproduce
The ocean separated the groups, so gene flow was stopped
The palms evolved into separate species within one generation
Pollen rarely passed between the groups, so their gene pools diverged
questions.explanation: Different flowering times meant that pollen from one group seldom reached flowers of the other, so gene flow between them was greatly reduced. With little gene flow, selection and drift caused the gene pools to diverge until the groups were reproductively isolated. No ocean separated them, which is why the case is sympatric.

questions.stem: Two populations of frogs separated by a river are brought together. They mate, but their hybrid offspring are always sterile. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: They are one species, because sterile offspring show close relatedness
They are still one species, because they share a common ancestor
They have become separate species through reproductive isolation
They are still one species because they were able to mate
questions.explanation: Producing only sterile hybrids means the gene pools can no longer mix, so the populations are reproductively isolated and are separate species. Mating alone is not enough; the offspring must be fertile. Sharing a common ancestor does not make populations one species; all species share ancestors at some point.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of a human, a whale and a bat have the same arrangement of bones but different functions. What are they?
options: Homologous structures
Analogous structures
Vestigial structures
Transitional structures
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share a basic structure inherited from a common ancestor, even though they are now used for grasping, swimming or flying. Analogous structures have a similar function but different structures and origins, such as the wings of a bird and an insect.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a vestigial structure?
options: The small pelvic bones of a whale
The wings of a bat
The flippers of a dolphin
The opposable thumb of a human
questions.explanation: A vestigial structure is reduced and has lost most or all of its original function. Whales have tiny pelvic bones, evidence that they descended from four-legged land mammals. Bat wings and dolphin flippers are functional homologous structures.

questions.stem: Why do the wings of a bird and a butterfly not show that the two are closely related?
options: They are analogous: similar function from different origins
They are homologous: similar structure from a common ancestor
They are vestigial: reduced structures that lost their function
They are transitional: features shared by ancestor and descendant
questions.explanation: Bird wings are modified forelimbs with bones, while butterfly wings are outgrowths of the exoskeleton, so they evolved separately to do the same job. This is convergent evolution, and analogous structures give no evidence of a recent common ancestor.

questions.stem: The amino acid sequence of cytochrome c is compared. Species W differs from humans at 1 position, species X at 12, and species Y at 21. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Y shares the most recent common ancestor with humans
X is the ancestor of both W and Y
W and Y are more closely related than W and X
W shares the most recent common ancestor with humans
questions.explanation: Differences in a protein's sequence build up over time after two lineages split, so fewer differences means a more recent common ancestor. W, with one difference, is most closely related to humans. Molecular comparisons show relatedness, not which living species is an ancestor of another.

questions.stem: Why is a comparison of DNA sequences often more informative than a comparison of amino acid sequences?
options: Because of degeneracy, some DNA changes do not alter the amino acid
Because DNA sequences are identical in every species compared
Because amino acid sequences change faster than DNA sequences
Because only DNA, not protein, is inherited from a common ancestor
questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate, so some mutations change the DNA without changing the amino acid. DNA comparisons detect these silent differences, as well as those in non-coding regions, giving finer detail. Amino acid sequences change more slowly, not faster, than DNA.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, what does a node where two branches split represent?
options: A mass extinction that ended both of the lineages
The point at which a fossil of each species was found
The most recent common ancestor of the two lineages
A species that is still alive today in both lineages
questions.explanation: Each node is a divergence point, the common ancestor from which the two branches descend. Living species are at the tips of the branches, not at the nodes.

questions.stem: In a phylogenetic tree, species P and Q share a node that is more recent than the node P shares with R. Which statement follows?
options: P is more closely related to R than to Q
Q evolved from P after the split with R
R is the common ancestor of P and Q
P is more closely related to Q than to R
questions.explanation: Relatedness is read from how recently two species share a common ancestor. P and Q split from each other after their lineage had split from R, so P and Q are more closely related. Species at the tips are living relatives, not ancestors of one another.

questions.stem: A student says that because species S is drawn next to species T at the tips of a tree, they must be closely related. Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: Species drawn next to each other are always the least related
Tip position shows the age of each species, not relatedness
Only species at the top of a tree can be related to each other
Branches can rotate at a node, so tip order does not show relatedness
questions.explanation: A tree can be rotated around any node without changing the relationships it shows, so two tips can be side by side yet distantly related. Relatedness is read by tracing back to the most recent shared node.

questions.stem: Which pair of features is shared by all mammals?
options: A lack of a tail and a broad chest
Bipedalism and a large brain
Hair and mammary glands
Opposable thumbs and nails
questions.explanation: All mammals have hair at some stage of life and females have mammary glands that produce milk. Opposable thumbs and nails are primate features, the loss of a tail is a hominoid feature, and habitual bipedalism defines hominins.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of primates and gives them depth perception?
options: A large nose and a strong sense of smell
A tail used to grip branches when climbing
Forward-facing eyes with overlapping fields of view
Eyes on the sides of the head for all-round vision
questions.explanation: Forward-facing eyes give overlapping images, producing stereoscopic vision that lets primates judge distance, which suits life in trees. Eyes on the sides of the head give a wide view but poor depth perception; primates rely less on smell than many mammals.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes hominoids, the apes and humans, from other primates such as monkeys?
options: Forward-facing eyes
Nails instead of claws
Opposable thumbs
The absence of a tail
questions.explanation: Hominoids have no tail, along with a broad, flat chest and a highly mobile shoulder joint. Forward-facing eyes, nails and opposable thumbs are shared by primates generally, including monkeys.

questions.stem: In a hominin skull, the foramen magnum is positioned centrally underneath. In a chimpanzee it is further back. What does this show about the hominin?
options: It walked on its knuckles, like a chimpanzee walks today
It had a larger brain than any member of the genus Homo
It had a long tail used for balance while moving on two legs
It walked upright, with its skull balanced on a vertical spine
questions.explanation: The foramen magnum is where the spinal cord enters the skull. A central, forward position means the skull sat on top of a vertical spine, a sign of habitual bipedalism, the defining hominin feature. A rear position suits a quadruped whose spine is roughly horizontal.

questions.stem: Which change in brain size is seen from the genus Australopithecus to modern Homo sapiens?
options: An increase from about 400–500 cm³ to about 1350 cm³
A decrease from about 1350 cm³ to about 400–500 cm³
No real change, staying at about 1350 cm³ throughout
An increase from about 100 cm³ to about 400–500 cm³
questions.explanation: Australopithecines had brains similar in size to a chimpanzee's, around 400–500 cm³, while modern humans average about 1350 cm³. The increase was a major trend within the genus Homo. Treat these as approximate, because brain sizes vary within each species.

questions.stem: Compared with Australopithecus, how did limb structure change in later members of the genus Homo?
options: Legs became shorter relative to arms, and the big toe became opposable
Arms and legs stayed in the same proportions, but fingers became curved
Arms became shorter relative to legs, and fingers became straighter
Arms became longer relative to legs, and fingers became more curved
questions.explanation: Australopithecines kept fairly long arms and curved fingers, features useful for climbing, while later Homo species had shorter arms relative to their longer legs and straighter fingers, suiting full-time life on the ground. An opposable big toe is an ape feature, lost in hominins.

questions.stem: Which evidence supports interbreeding between Homo sapiens and Homo neanderthalensis?
options: Neanderthal skulls are identical in shape to modern human skulls
Neanderthals and modern humans have never been found in the same region
Modern humans carry Neanderthal mtDNA passed down through mothers
Neanderthal DNA matches sections of many living humans' genomes
questions.explanation: Sequencing DNA from Neanderthal bones revealed segments that are also found in the genomes of many living people, especially those whose ancestors lived outside Africa, which is best explained by interbreeding. No Neanderthal mtDNA has been found in living humans. Neanderthal skulls differ in shape from ours.

questions.stem: When fossils of small-bodied hominins were found on the island of Flores, some scientists named a new species, Homo floresiensis, while others disagreed. What does this show?
options: Classification of hominins can be contested and revised as evidence grows
Classification of hominins is fixed once a species has been named
Classification of hominins depends only on the size of the body
Classification of hominins cannot use fossils, only living populations
questions.explanation: The human fossil record is a classification scheme open to differing interpretations, and new finds can challenge, refine or replace existing ideas. Debate about whether a find is a new species or a variant of a known one is a normal part of science. Classification uses many features, not body size alone.

questions.stem: Why is mitochondrial DNA useful for tracing the migration of modern human populations?
options: It is inherited only from the mother and does not recombine
It is inherited from both parents and mixes in every generation
It never mutates, so all humans carry an identical sequence
It is found only in the nucleus of a person's egg cells
questions.explanation: Because mtDNA passes down the maternal line without recombination, changes in it come only from mutation, so lineages can be traced and compared. The greatest mtDNA diversity is found in African populations, consistent with modern humans arising in Africa and migrating outward.
